messages.author: a0b9933f22c7c64f
messages.subject: Power analysis - comparing methods
parts:
Hi all,

I'm interested in completing a power analysis for a study that compares methods in occupancy studies. I have reviewed several of Guillera - Arroita's papers, including the 2012 publication, and have used their developed R code to run power analyses. However, that paper concentrates on changes in occupancy over seasons. In my case, I'm interested in single-season data. I expect detection probabilities to differ significantly between the two methods, thus improving my estimate of psi, but I don't expect true occupancy or habitat use to change as it is only comparing data from a single season. Any help is very much appreciated.

Best,
Brent

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Power analysis - comparing methods
parts:
Hi Brent,

As you've read, for a power analysis you need to simulate data under certain conditions and fit models to see how well you are able to estimate parameters of interest.  If you've got R code for an occupancy-based power analysis, adapting it to your questions involves selecting a range of sampling conditions, estimating occupancy and/or covariate relationships under multiple (e.g., >100) data replicates, and calculating RMSE or some other metric of accuracy.  If you have J sites and assume some occupancy probability psi, you could sample an increasing proportion of sites (e.g., J/5, J/4, etc.) across different detection surveys (with varying p or whatever) to examine how many sites need to be sampled to estimate psi with some degree of accuracy under the different survey protocols.  You can make the focus whatever you want, depending on the question.

Hi Brent, 

you already got some good advice there. Just a note that our 2012 paper is not limited to seasons. The idea is to assess power to detect changes in occupancy among two samples of data, so could be from two seasons, but also e.g. two different places... 

G
